summary: The machine has the runtime, the DocumentDB MCP server, and the DocumentDB agent skills required to build the Python + Beanie + LangChain sample against an existing Azure DocumentDB cluster. Most factual gaps in the cold answers were resolvable from installed skills and Microsoft Learn. Remaining work for the implementer: pick LLM & embedding provider/models (which fixes embedding dimension and index params), supply or generate seeded sample data, and optionally run a local DocumentDB gateway for offline dev. No unavailable required tool blocks an initial build, but a few accelerators and CLI tools would speed development and testing.
summary_points: All essential run-time tools to write and run the sample are present: python, pip, docker, git, node/npx; the documentdb MCP server and Microsoft Learn search tools are available.

Installed DocumentDB agent skills provide authoritative guidance for deployment, connection strings, vector-index syntax (cosmosSearch), security/Entra auth, local gateway image and port, and driver initialization (Beanie + Motor).

Many cold answers were incorrect because they described Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or older naming; the correct facts (resource type = Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, vCore compute tiers, auth via MONGODB-OIDC, cosmosSearch index syntax, gateway port 10260, etc.) are documented in the installed skills and Microsoft Learn pages.

Missing decisions required before code is final: which embedding model & embedding dimension, which LLM/provider, and whether to seed real or synthetic data — these are policy/choice gaps, not missing infrastructure.

Accelerators that would speed building (local DocumentDB container running, and mongosh for ad-hoc checks) are absent or not running; MCP tools cover most verification needs so the build can start without them.
No tool reported unavailable is a hard blocker; the build proceeds with small workarounds and clarified facts.

tools.workaround: Install Python on the machine or run inside a container; none needed here.

tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure subscription, resource providers, optionally to provision clusters or firewall rules if required during development.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1; cosmosdb-preview/documentd listed among extensions in the inventory detail.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify subscription/provider registration and manage infra; but not required to run the sample against an existing cluster.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB accounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are deployed as resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API version examples shown in docs). The older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource type is for Azure Cosmos DB accounts, a different resource model.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap in marketing/branding; many Cosmos DB docs use databaseAccounts which looks similar to DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb commands or ARM templates that target databaseAccounts would not create the vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters resources the sample expects; deployment & index APIs would not match.
improvements: Clarify on the Azure DocumentDB quickstart pages and the top-level README that the managed DocumentDB cluster resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Add a deprecation/rename note on older cosmos-mongodb (vCore) docs pointing users to mongoClusters resource & az documentdb mongocluster commands.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI command group for the vCore DocumentDB product is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show). The az documentdb commands are the current documented CLI surface for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The MongoDB API on older Cosmos DB accounts used az cosmosdb; the new vCore product exposes az documentdb mongocluster commands. Shared words (cosmosdb / documentdb) cause overlap.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb CLI docs (older Cosmos DB account docs)

confusions.build_risk: If a builder runs az cosmosdb commands or follows those quickstarts, they will target Cosmos DB account APIs (databaseAccounts), not the mongoClusters API; provisioning or parameter choices will be incorrect.
improvements: On any 'create cluster' quickstart or sample, prefer and call out az documentdb mongocluster examples and mention the older az cosmosdb commands are for Cosmos DB accounts.
Add a short CLI migration note on the top-level DocumentDB quickstart that explicitly maps the legacy az cosmosdb flows to az documentdb mongocluster where applicable.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (kind=MongoDB).
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform resource types for the vCore DocumentDB product target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep) and Terraform's azurerm_mongo_cluster (or azapi/azurerm modules that target mongoClusters). Using databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account targets the Cosmos DB account resource (different product).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Terraform/Bicep examples for Cosmos DB MongoDB (RU) used databaseAccounts; the new vCore cluster resource uses the mongoClusters resource path.
confusions.build_risk: Applying a Bicep/Terraform template targeting databaseAccounts would create the wrong resource type; IaC and CI would be provisioned incorrectly.
improvements: Update IaC quickstarts to show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for DocumentDB vCore and add a short section that maps older databaseAccounts examples to the new resource when relevant.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB's connection strings for the vCore mongoClusters use MongoDB SRV/standard forms with the DocumentDB cluster host naming. The officially documented form (from the deployment skill) uses mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (note tls=true, authMechanism / OIDC options for Entra auth). For local gateway the port is typically 10260 (gateway image) — not 10255 used by the Cosmos DB databaseAccounts endpoint.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (connection strings)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cosmos.azure.com host and port 10255 are associated with legacy Cosmos DB accounts; DocumentDB vCore uses different host naming and SRV patterns, and the local gateway uses port 10260.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo connection string examples (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port or leaving driver defaults (e.g., retryWrites enabled) could cause connection failures. Using SRV vs non-SRV also changes how drivers resolve seed hosts.
improvements: Add a short Connection String Quick Reference to the top-level DocumentDB quickstart that lists SRV vs non-SRV examples, explains the required query params (tls/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local), and warns about retryWrites defaults.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units per second, RUs). You can provision fixed RUs, use autoscale RUs, or serverless mode.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore product) is a vCore/compute-tier model (M10, M20, M30, etc.) with compute tiers and storage; it is not the RU-based Cosmos DB billing model. Azure Cosmos DB (RU model) remains a separate offering. Choose M10..M200 compute tiers when provisioning DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services offer a MongoDB-compatible API and historically lived under the Cosmos brand; the RU model is the Cosmos DB throughput model, while the vCore model is the DocumentDB cluster billing model.
confusions.build_risk: If the implementer assumes RU-based limits they will pick wrong scaling and cost estimates, choose inappropriate index/IO tuning, or attempt to use serverless features not supported on the chosen cluster.
improvements: Clarify the billing model on the quickstart: state explicitly 'DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers (M10..M200) and storage; Cosmos DB (RU) is billed in RUs and is a different product/API option.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane access is typically via MongoDB credentials (username/password / SCRAM auth). Azure AD authentication for the MongoDB wire protocol is not the usual data-plane path.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) users and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) data-plane authentication; the service supports registering managed identities and connecting using an OIDC flow (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC connection properties). Drivers that implement the OIDC mechanism or tools that allow OIDC (MongoDB Compass, mongosh with OIDC support) can authenticate with Entra. The documentdb-security skill and docs provide examples.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB deployments rely only on user/password SCRAM; Entra/OIDC is an Azure-specific capability that not all MongoDB docs emphasize, leading to the assumption it's unsupported.
confusions.build_risk: If the implementer assumes Entra ID is unavailable they may hardcode credentials instead of using a managed identity, increasing operational risk. Conversely, assuming driver OIDC support without verifying the driver version may cause authentication failures.
improvements: Add a short 'how to connect with Entra' snippet in the DocumentDB quickstart and in the driver skill with the exact connection string examples (showing authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and required authMechanismProperties).
Document driver-version minimums for OIDC (e.g., mongosh/driver versions that support MONGODB-OIDC) in the driver best-practices page.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo or motor for Python). For async ODM in Python use Beanie (which runs on Motor). There is not a separate data-plane Cosmos-specific MongoDB client; management/ARM operations use azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / azure-identity.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor) for data-plane access; Beanie on top of Motor is appropriate for an async ODM in Python. Management/control-plane ops use Azure management SDKs. The documentdb-driver and init_beanie examples in the skills show the correct initialization pattern.

grounding_links.title: Init Beanie with Motor example (Beanie + Motor + DocumentDB)

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: You create an index on the embedding field using createIndex with engine-specific options (HNSW/IVF). Example: db.complaints.createIndex( { embedding: 1 }, { name: 'emb_hnsw', algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' ... } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB uses the cosmosSearch vector index family (kinds: vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf). The correct createIndex form uses { embedding: 'cosmosSearch' } with cosmosSearchOptions in the index definition. Example from the vector-search skill: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, { name: 'products_embedding_diskann', cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-diskann', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', maxDegree: 32, lBuild: 50 } }).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic community createIndex key names (algorithm/dims) that look like self-hosted implementations; DocumentDB exposes a cosmosSearch index type with specific 'cosmosSearchOptions' properties.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong createIndex syntax or wrong option names will fail or silently produce a non-functional index. Mismatched dimensions (index vs embeddings) will produce silent incorrect search results.
improvements: Document the exact createIndex form for cosmosSearch in the 'indexing' quick examples and show a minimal createIndex snippet for HNSW and DiskANN with required fields (dimensions, similarity).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes (db.coll.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) or integrate Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid search.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB's full-text search uses createSearchIndexes + the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring, analyzers, fuzzy/phrase operators). Hybrid search (lexical + vector) is supported by using the DocumentDB search indexes and combining $search with cosmosSearch or merging results in-app; you do not rely on MongoDB's community text index or a separate Cognitive Search service for integrated hybrid search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: MongoDB community text indexes are the historical way to do basic text search in MongoDB; DocumentDB provides a separate, more capable search subsystem with different commands and a $search stage.
confusions.build_risk: If the implementer uses community text indexes instead of createSearchIndexes/$search they will miss BM25 scoring features and hybrid (vector+lexical) patterns DocumentDB supports, and queries may not perform as expected.
improvements: Add an explicit 'don't use db.createIndex({text})' short note in the DocumentDB quickstarts and show an end-to-end $search example with an index creation snippet.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports particular wire protocol versions depending on account config; historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and more recently 6/7 previews; some features limited (server-side JS/eval, some aggregation stages, certain admin commands).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (per current docs) and advertises ~99.03% operator compatibility. Some administrative commands are not exposed and a small set of operators or stages may differ; the compatibility pages list details. The service is designed to work with MongoDB drivers that support the listed wire protocols.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (MQL compatibility)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older Cosmos account compatibility statements. The correct supported versions are documented and include 5.0–8.0.
confusions.build_risk: Using a driver that only supports older/newer wire versions might cause incompatibilities; always check driver/server version pairing and test critical features against the target cluster version.
improvements: Document the driver minimum version matrix for OIDC/auth and wire-protocol compatibility in the driver skill page so implementers pick a compatible pymongo/motor/Beanie stack.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator) and Mongo endpoint commonly port 10255 for TLS. Alternatively use official mongo Docker image.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB development the recommended local gateway image is ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and the PG endpoint on 9712). The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator is not the right local image for the DocumentDB open-source engine; the documentdb-local-deployment skill documents the gateway image and port 10260.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Cosmos DB emulator historically mimics older Cosmos DB APIs; the new DocumentDB product publishes a Gateway image and a different local port. Many blog posts conflate them.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to run the Cosmos emulator or using the wrong port will not reproduce DocumentDB behaviors (vector indexes, Entra auth simulation, gateway TLS specifics) and leads to wasted debugging time.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' section to the quickstart showing the Gateway image and the exact Docker command/compose with port 10260 and TLS relax guidance for integration tests.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are available depending on the MongoDB wire version; $changeStream may be available; no separate portal toggle usually required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For some cluster topologies (e.g., multishard clusters) a portal-preview setting or feature flag (Change streams for multishard clusters) may need to be enabled; the migration and Mongoose docs explain the requirement. The DocumentDB docs include a 'Change streams' how-to and notes on enabling the feature for particular cluster modes.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change streams are a MongoDB concept and availability depends on the service and cluster configuration; older docs do not always call out the portal/feature toggle for multishard clusters.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are always on may break an online-migration or streaming pipeline; check the cluster settings and enable the DocumentDB change-streams feature when needed.
improvements: Add a small note in the change-streams doc listing when a portal/preview feature must be enabled (e.g., multishard clusters) and how to detect it programmatically.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (profile name 'documentdb') for data-plane inspection tools. The general Azure MCP server covers many services, but the documentdb MCP server has service-specific tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the inventory includes a 'documentdb' MCP server with data-plane tools (list DBs, createIndex, aggregate, explain, etc.). The general Azure MCP server exists for control-plane operations, but the documentdb MCP server is the right data-plane toolset for collection/index/plan inspection.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally branded the service as DocumentDB. It evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated; 'DocumentDB' was Microsoft's original product name before rebranding to Cosmos DB which now offers multiple APIs including SQL (DocumentDB), Gremlin, Table, Cassandra and the MongoDB-compatible API.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a common source of confusion. The current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' is the vCore rebranding of the earlier 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'; it is distinct from the older 'Azure DocumentDB' product (2014–2017) that became Azure Cosmos DB. The new Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. In short: (1) 'Azure DocumentDB' (current) = vCore product, (2) 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)' = RU-based Cosmos offering, (3) the original 2014–2017 DocumentDB rebranded to Cosmos DB historically. The open-source DocumentDB engine is the codebase powering the new product.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Overlapping product names and a rebrand history (the old DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB, then 'vCore' flavor -> renamed to Azure DocumentDB) plus similar API labels cause mistaken identity between products and versions.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB vs DocumentDB product pages

confusions.build_risk: Following historic docs that mention 'DocumentDB' without date/context may lead a builder to use wrong APIs or resource types (databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters).
improvements: Add a concise 'naming and compatibility timeline' callout to top-level docs clarifying the three items (original DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB; Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU); vCore product renamed to Azure DocumentDB) and mapping resource/CLI paths for each.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the backing engine is Cosmos DB's own storage/engine. For most CRUD and basic aggregation queries, MongoDB drivers work unchanged. However some features differ and must be tested.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore DocumentDB product the engine is the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. Application code using MongoDB drivers, Beanie/Motor, or standard MongoDB shims will generally work; test and verify a small set of incompatibilities documented in the compatibility pages. The implementation details (engine name) do not force code changes beyond connection strings and feature checks.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.question: What exact connection string and environment variable should the sample use to reach the cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment. Expect a Mongo-style URI on TLS and port 10255, e.g. mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. Use motor.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (as the run environment instructs). For the vCore DocumentDB cluster the documented connection string uses mongodb+srv or mongodb schemes with the cluster host (e.g., <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and TLS (tls=true). The documented example shows mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. For local gateway use port 10260 and appropriate TLS flags.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: create cluster & view connection strings

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used Cosmos DB databaseAccounts host suffix and port 10255; the vCore cluster uses a different naming convention and SRV host. The environment var name (DOCUMENTDB_URI) is correct in the prompt.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo connection string examples

confusions.build_risk: If the app expects port 10255 or a cosmos databaseAccounts host, it may fail to connect to the mongoClusters endpoint or use wrong connection options (SRV vs non-SRV).
improvements: Add the correct example value (with the cluster host naming and SRV example) to the sample's .env.example so implementers get the right format without guessing.

confusions.question: Which database and collection names will the sample create and operate on?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_banking_14. Create/operate on at least two collections: complaints (raw and enriched complaint documents) and complaint_embeddings (or complaints with an embedding field).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the run environment explicitly asked to use database sample_banking_14. The implementer may choose to use a single complaints collection with an embedding field or separate collection for embeddings; the sample's prompt and skills support either pattern. documentdb-data-modeling skill advises embedding vectors into the same document (common pattern) unless there are specific write/read contention reasons.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW parameters: db.complaints.createIndex( { embedding: 1 }, { name: 'emb_hnsw', algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the cosmosSearch index type and createIndex with cosmosSearchOptions. Example from the vector-search skill: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, { name: 'products_embedding_diskann', cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-diskann' | 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-ivf', dimensions: <dims>, similarity: 'COS'|'L2'|'IP', maxDegree: <int>, lBuild: <int> } }). Ensure 'dimensions' exactly matches the chosen embedding model output.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer used different (community) createIndex option names (algorithm/dims) and numeric attributes that differ from DocumentDB's cosmosSearchOptions structure.
confusions.build_risk: Wrong index syntax or mismatched dimensions will break similarity search silently or cause index creation failure.
improvements: Add an in-repo example index-creation script that uses cosmosSearchOptions with a placeholder for 'dimensions' tied to the .env.example embedding_model choice.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will surface complaint hotspots by category?
confusions.cold_answer: Pipeline: [ { $match: { category: { $exists: true } } }, { $group: { _id: '$category', count: { $sum: 1 }, topComplaints: { $push: { id: '$_id', text: '$text', urgency: '$urgency' } } } }, { $sort: { count: -1 } }, { $project: { category: '$_id', count: 1, topComplaints: { $slice: ['$topComplaints', 5] } } } ].
confusions.grounded_answer: The aggregation pipeline is valid and appropriate for DocumentDB. It will surface counts per category and top complaints per category. Use documentdb_aggregate or a driver aggregate() call to run it; for large collections consider a $limit before $push or use $top/$topN accumulation patterns if supported for memory efficiency.

confusions.question: How will the app authenticate and initialize Beanie ODM in Python?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Motor with the MongoDB connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass the Motor client to Beanie: AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']); await init_beanie(database=client['sample_banking_14'], document_models=[Complaint]).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use Motor's AsyncIOMotorClient initialized with DOCUMENTDB_URI and call beanie.init_beanie(database=client['sample_banking_14'], document_models=[...]). Also follow documentdb-driver guidance: reuse a singleton client, set driver options recommended for DocumentDB (e.g., retryWrites=false), and read credentials from env/Key Vault.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when referring to or provisioning the vCore DocumentDB product; create/migration examples and CLI commands must use az documentdb mongocluster and the mongoClusters ARM type.

Create vector indexes using the cosmosSearch index type and cosmosSearchOptions (dimensions must exactly match your embedding model) — do not copy Atlas or community createIndex option names; use the example form in the vector-search skill.

Authenticate drivers either with SCRAM user/password or Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC). If you plan to use Entra, verify driver/tool OIDC support and use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC with the required authMechanismProperties; store secrets in Key Vault or use managed identity instead of embedding passwords.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (no new app-level end-to-end Azure deployment is needed). If the team wanted a full app deployment template, install azd per https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/azure-dev to simplify app scaffolding.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful only if you plan to provision clusters from this machine; the run policy forbids Azure writes in many runs. If you do want IaC locally, install bicep CLI (learn quickstart) or rely on the Bicep templates included in documentdb-azure-deployment.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform helps if your repo will include example Terraform for mongoClusters; otherwise you can rely on Bicep or the provided examples. Install Terraform only if you intend to demonstrate IaC provisioning from this machine.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for a Python + Beanie sample. Add only if you plan to produce a .NET variant of the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh (or MongoDB Compass) to allow quick ad-hoc inspection and manual queries of the cluster. If installing is undesirable, use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation) as the programmatic alternative. To install mongosh, use the MongoDB download/install instructions or the package manager for your OS.
